extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and students of natural philosophy (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and methods in classical celestial mechanics: computing lunar and solar forces on the seas, the Moon's figure and gravity, precession of the equinoxes, location and motion of comets, and geometric/analytic lemmas for constructing parabolic curves through observed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII. Prob. XVII. Invenire vim Lunæ ad Mare movendum.
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to determine the Moon's force in moving the sea from its proportion to the Sun's force, inferred via proportions of observed tidal amplitudes (e.g., Avon and Plymouth observations: Syzygy vs Quadrature heights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton compares observed tide heights in Syzygy and Quadrature (examples: Avon: 45 ft vs 25 ft; Plymouth: 19¾ ft vs 12¼ ft) to deduce ratios L:S of lunar to solar tidal forces (two computations yield ~5-7/15:1 and ~7-1/3:1; adopts mean 6-1/3:1). Given Solar force relative to Earth's gravity (1:12,868,200), deduces Lunar force relative to gravity (1:2,031,821). The method shows how observational tide differences map to force ratios; Newton notes uncertainties and chooses an intermediate proportion until better observations are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. XXXVII) — tidal amplitudes and geographic dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: If solar force would raise water by one foot and eleven digits, the same lunar force would raise it by twelve feet; observed tidal amplitudes in large open seas (Pacific, Atlantic, Æthiopic) can be six, nine, twelve, or fifteen feet, larger in wider/deeper seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton explains how basin width, depth, and geometry influence observed tidal amplitude: wide/deep seas exhibit larger tides; narrow or shallow seas, or ports with strong inflow/outflow through shallow channels, can show greatly amplified local tides (examples: Plymouth, Chepstow, S. Michael, Cambaya, Pegu). He distinguishes places where local hydraulic effects dominate from open-sea responses matching the computed lunar/solar forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. XXXVII) — detectability of lunar tidal force
rubrics_metrics.description: With lunar force to gravity as 1:2,031,821, the lunar force is far too small to be felt in pendulum or static/hydrostatic experiments; it manifests sensibly only in the sea's tidal motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that the lunar tidal force is negligible in ordinary terrestrial laboratory experiments and only produces noticeable effects in the ocean (the only place where the small force accumulates into observable motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 3 (to Prop. XXXVII) — relation of densities of Moon, Sun, and Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Since lunar force on the sea is about 6-1/3 times the solar one and forces scale with apparent diameters and densities, Newton deduces density relations leading to Moon's density relative to Sun and Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using apparent diameters (Solar & Lunar) and previously deduced Solar:Earth density ratio (100:387), Newton computes lunar density ≈ 600:387 (≈9:5) relative to Earth, concluding the Moon is denser, more 'terrestrial' than Earth (derivation given in Latin with numerical apparent-diameter figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 4 (to Prop. XXXVII) — mass ratio Moon:Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the deduced densities and the Moon's true diameter relative to Earth (1:3.65 approx.), the mass of the Moon to Earth is about 1:26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines density and diameter relations to give an approximate Moon:Earth mass ratio; brief numerical conclusion without extended proof in this corollary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 5 (to Prop. XXXVII) — lunar surface gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The lunar surface gravity (accelerative gravity on Moon's surface) is roughly half that of Earth's surface gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion follows from previous density and size/mass relations; stated as a direct consequence rather than a derivation here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII. Prob. XVIII. Invenire figuram corporis Lunæ.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the lunar body were fluid like Earth's seas, the Earth's attraction would deform it so that the Moon's maximal diameter passing through Earth's center would exceed perpendicular diameters by about 180 feet, producing a spheroid whose major axis points to Earth and thus maintaining the same lunar face toward Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton reasons by symmetry (comparing amplitudes of sea tides and corresponding bulges in a fluid Moon under Earth's pull): if the Moon were fluid, Earth's pull on lunar fluid would raise bulges analogous to ocean tides, leading to a tidal elongation with largest diameter through the Earth; this shape explains synchronous rotation (the same face toward Earth), with any oscillations being exceedingly slow because the tidal forces are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma I — equivalence of particulate force distributions for rotating Earth/annulus
rubrics_metrics.description: If APEp denotes a uniformly dense Earth with center C and equator AE, and if an annulus described by radius CP exerts on a particle a tendency proportional to its distance from a plane QR (normal to the line from the Sun's center to Earth's center), then the total efficacy of all such particles to move the Earth circularly is one-fourth the efficacy of equal particles placed uniformly on the equatorial ring AE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton proves via decomposition of forces (LM into LN and NM) and shows ratios of resultant efficacies (three to two, etc.), culminating that the total effect of distributed particles is one-fourth that of the equatorial ring — used later in precession calculations. The lemma includes geometric configuration labels and a concise argument referencing earlier corollaries of the Laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II — ratio of Earth's rotation (composed) to annulus rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion of the entire Earth about the given axis, composed from motions of its parts, is to the motion of an annulus (of equal matter) about the same axis in a ratio compounded from the ratio of masses and a numerical factor (given as 925275 : 1000000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton relates motions of a cylinder and its inscribed sphere and thin annulus to obtain the composite ratio; the lemma supplies the mechanical factor needed to relate the effect of distributed mass to equivalent annular motion in later precession computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma III — equivalence of motion of annulus whether fluid or rigid
rubrics_metrics.description: If an annulus (with all other Earth removed) were carried annually about the Sun while rotating daily with its axis inclined to the ecliptic, the motion of its equinoctial points would be the same whether the annulus were fluid or rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that for the purpose of determining the motion of equinox points, the physical rigidity or fluidity of the annulus does not change the effect — justifies treating distributed matter as annular elements when computing precession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIX. Prob. XIX. Invenire Præcessionem Æquinoctiorum.
rubrics_metrics.description: Computation of the annual precession of the equinoxes arising from solar and lunar actions on Earth's equatorial bulge and annular mass distributions, leading to a theoretical value (~49"58') close to observed ~50".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton combines lunar node motion in a modeled annulus, ratios from Lemmas I–III, numerical factors (e.g., 1436:39343, 4143:443391), and corrections for Earth's density distribution and obliquity (use of sinus complement 91706/100000 radius) to derive the precession. He also discusses how variations in Earth's density (altitude of equatorial mass) affect the computed value and chooses intermediate ratios producing an annual precession near 49"58', matching astronomical observation (~50").

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma IV — Comets are beyond the Moon and inhabit planetary regions
rubrics_metrics.description: From lack of diurnal parallax and annual parallax behavior, apparent retrograde/prograde/acceleration patterns, and brightness/size of comet heads and tails, Newton concludes comets lie above the lunar region, in the planetary domain (often within or near Saturn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include: parallaxes (diurnal and annual) showing comets are more distant than the lunar region; apparent motion changes produced by Earth's motion analogous to planetary retrogradations; brightness and apparent diameters of comet heads and coma compared to planets (Flamsteed, Hevelius observations) indicating comets are not in the fixed stars but nearer (often near or inside Saturn's orbit). Newton also discusses effects of coma/fumes on apparent brightness and tail illumination mechanisms (reflection vs. emitted light), and uses temporal brightness changes with approach/recession to infer solar proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XL. Theor. XXI — comets move in conic sections with Sun at focus and sweep areas proportional to times
rubrics_metrics.description: Comets move in conic sections (parabolas, ellipses, hyperbolas depending on energy) having the Sun at a focus and describe equal areas in equal times (Kepler's area law applied to comets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries: (1) If comets return their orbits will be ellipses and periods scale as the 3/2 power of transverse axes; e.g., if a comet's axis is four times Saturn's, its period ~240 years. (2) Orbits of comets are often close to parabolas, so parabolic approximations are usually adequate. (3) Velocity relation: comet velocity at a given solar distance is proportional to planetary velocity at that distance by the inverse square-root ratio of distances. Newton gives numerical examples using large integer radii and Earth motion numbers to compute diurnal and hourly motions for comets at Earth's distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma V — construct a parabolic curve through arbitrarily given points
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to find a parabola passing through given points A, B, C, D, E, F,... by dropping perpendiculars to a given line HN, computing finite differences (first, second, third, ...), and forming the ordinate series RS = a + bp + cq + dr + es + ft + ... (cases for equal and unequal abscissa intervals provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case 1 treats equal abscissa intervals; Case 2 treats unequal intervals by dividing difference quantities by the interval lengths. The lemma gives an explicit finite-difference procedure (with notation for successive differences labeled b, c, d, f, etc.) and a recipe to build the ordinate RS by successively adding scaled terms (p, q, r...). Corollary: areas under curves can be approximated by the area of the parabola found through sampled points (useful for quadrature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma VI — interpolate comet location at an intermediate time from observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given observed longitudes (and latitudes) at several times, draw a regular curve through those points (using Lemma V) and evaluate its ordinate at the desired intermediate time to find the comet's longitude/latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from observation intervals HI, IK, KL, LM and observed longitudes HA, IB, KC, LD, ME, use Lemma V to construct RS (the ordinate) and take RS as the needed longitude at time HS. Newton notes that if observed longitude differences are small (e.g., 4–5'), three or four observations suffice; if differences are larger (10–20'), five observations are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma VII — construct a line through a given point with segments PB:PC in a given ratio relative to two given lines AB and AC
rubrics_metrics.description: Through a given point P, to draw a straight line BC such that the parts PB and PC, when projected on two given lines AB and AC respectively, have a prescribed ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: from P draw any PD towards one of the given lines and extend to E so that PE:PD equals the required ratio; draw EC parallel to AD to get the desired proportionality, then CPB yields PC:PB = PE:PD. Short geometric construction with Q.E.F. (quod erat faciendum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma VIII — chord segment proportionality to time for a parabola
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parabola ABC with focus S, if chord AC is bisected at I and I[mu] is the diameter to vertex [mu] with [mu]O = 1/2 I[mu], then for a comet moving on arc CBA the point E where line [xi]B (constructed as specified) cuts AC will cut off AE approximately proportional to the time taken to sweep that arc (i.e., AE:AC ≈ time ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton gives a geometric construction tying areas and triangles to show that AE:AC is approximately the ratio of times for the corresponding arcs. The proof relies on area equality approximations and properties of the constructed points [xi], O, and similar triangles; used in approximating time-arc relations for parabolic motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma IX — relationship of certain parabola lines and rectitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: The lines I[mu], [mu]M, and the length AIC divided by 4S[mu] are equal; 4S[mu] is the latus rectum of the parabola associated with vertex B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short geometric identity about parabola elements used in subsequent lemmas to relate chord lengths, tangents, and areas; stated as an equality without extended elaboration here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma X — when arc equals chord under a particular velocity assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: If SP is extended to N and P such that [mu]N is one third of [mu]I and SP:SN = SN:S[mu], then the comet, during the time it describes arc A[mu]C with the instantaneous velocity at altitude SP kept equal to that at S[mu], would describe a length equal to the chord AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues by comparing the area swept by the radius and the triangular/arc areas to show that under that velocity scaling (velocity inversely proportional to radius in certain proportion), the arc-length described in that time equals the straight chord AC; the lemma supports approximations relating tangential distances to chord lengths under specified velocity laws.
